title: Algorithmic Fairness in Mortgage Lending: from Absolute Conditions to Relational Trade-offs
abstract: Abstract To address the rising concern that algorithmic decision-making may reinforce discriminatory biases, researchers have proposed many notions of fairness and corresponding mathematical formalizations. Each of these notions is often presented as a one-size-fits-all, absolute condition; however, in reality, the practical and ethical trade-offs are unavoidable and more complex. We introduce a new approach that considers fairness—not as a binary, absolute mathematical condition—but rather, as a relational notion in comparison to alternative decisionmaking processes. Using US mortgage lending as an example use case, we discuss the ethical foundations of each definition of fairness and demonstrate that our proposed methodology more closely captures the ethical trade-offs of the decision-maker, as well as forcing a more explicit representation of which values and objectives are prioritised.

claims.text: Moving from Naïve Bayes to Random Forest reduces the loan denial rate for black applicants by 10.7 percentage points.
Moving from Naïve Bayes to Random Forest yields 368 additional median-value loans totaling $55.27 million in expected value.
CART achieves $15.6 million more expected loan value compared to Logistic Regression.
CART results in a 3.8 percentage points higher denial rate for black loan applicants compared to Logistic Regression.
Including applicant race in feature sets produces a statistically significant accuracy increase for Random Forest (t = 4.04, p = 0.0029).
Including applicant race in feature sets produces a statistically significant accuracy decrease for Naïve Bayes (t = -6.22, p = 0.00015).
Including applicant race in feature sets produces a statistically significant accuracy increase for CART (t = 2.41, p = 0.040).
Applicants holding an FHA-insured loan type have a 36.16% probability of being black, compared to 19.38% for non-FHA-insured loan types.

limitations.text: The public HMDA dataset lacks actual default outcomes, credit scores, and full interest rate terms, limiting the internal validity of empirical loan approval analysis.
The framework assumes a simplified single-lender model with a static $1B capital limit, ignoring competitive market-level dynamics across multiple lenders.
Existing mathematical fairness definitions impose generalisable absolute thresholds that fail to account for pre-existing structural bias embedded in historical training data.

future_work.text: Expand the trade-off framework to market-level multi-player models incorporating regulators and aggregated lender decisions.
Generalise the relational trade-off methodology to other domains such as hiring, insurance pricing, and criminal recidivism.

methodologies.name: Relational Algorithmic Trade-off Analysis
methodologies.description: Evaluates predictive algorithms by quantifying trade-offs between domain-specific objective measures (such as financial inclusion expected value versus minority denial rate) across competing models rather than applying absolute pass/fail mathematical fairness thresholds.
